what_worked: Strong thesis with a clear investor audience; the crowding-vs-median-revenue contrast is genuinely useful.
fix_next: Multiple median values are materially wrong versus the reference data—verify every number against the actual dataset before presenting.
verdict: Compelling narrative undermined by several wrong figures and narrow scope.
factual_error_detail: Slide 1: Combined MRR stated as $13.5M; actual total 30-day revenue is $15,596,344.59 (~$15.6M). Slide 3: AI share of revenue stated as 13.4%; actual is $2,356,676/$15,596,345 = 15.1%. Slide 4: Median values are systematically wrong—Marketing shown $1,586 vs reference $2,369.50; Content Creation $1,254 vs $1,237.50 (close but off); AI $446 vs $503; Health & Fitness $392 vs $662.50; SaaS $303 vs $200.50; Mobile Apps $223 vs $232.50; Dev Tools $185 vs $635; Productivity $42 vs $79.91. At least 5 of 8 medians are materially wrong (Marketing, AI, H&F, Dev Tools, SaaS direction even reverses relative ranking). Slide 7: Education median $2,142 vs reference $2,435; Analytics $1,294 vs $419—Analytics is very wrong. Slide 5: 66% concentration claim for top-10 AI is unverifiable but plausible given skew. Slide 6: r=0.30 for followers vs MRR is unverifiable from provided reference but presented without caveats on what variable pair was used.

evidence.insight: The core insight—crowded categories yield worse median outcomes—is genuinely decision-useful for an investor audience (slides 3-5). However, the deck doesn't go much deeper: no B2B/B2C split, no provider analysis, no discussion of what distinguishes the AI winners from losers. The hype-vs-traction point (slide 6) is interesting but relies on two cherry-picked anecdotes rather than systematic analysis.
evidence.narrative: Clean arc: gold rush → median reality → concentration → hype disconnect → alternatives → takeaway. Each slide advances the thesis logically. The landing on slide 8 synthesizes well. Loses half a point for being somewhat narrow—one thesis explored from only one angle without counterarguments or alternative explanations.
evidence.framing: Audience (investor/due-diligence) is clear from title and language. Dataset source and freeze date are cited consistently. However: 274 missing category values are never disclosed, which matters enormously when the entire argument rests on category comparisons. The denominator issue (726 categorized out of 1,000) is invisible to the reader. Slide 7 uses n=5 and n=7 categories without flagging statistical fragility.
evidence.accuracy: Total revenue is wrong ($13.5M vs $15.6M). AI revenue share is wrong. Multiple category medians are materially incorrect—some by 2-3x (Dev Tools: $185 vs $635; Analytics: $1,294 vs $419). These errors undermine the core ranking argument: if Dev Tools actually has a higher median than AI, the narrative still holds but the specific comparisons are misleading. The SaaS median direction even reverses relative to some peers. At least 7 material factual errors across the deck.
evidence.visual: Consistent design system with navy/orange/teal palette. Good hierarchy with section labels, clear titles, and annotated charts. Donut charts on slides 3 and 5 are effective for part-to-whole. Bar chart on slide 4 uses color highlighting well. Slide 6 case-study layout is clean. Slide 7 horizontal bars work well for comparison. No chart junk. Minor issue: two donut charts on slide 3 could be replaced with a more precise comparison format.
evidence.ai_slop: Minimal slop. The deck is focused and avoids generic filler. The 'lottery ticket' metaphor on slide 5 is slightly overblown but grounded in a specific claim. Overall editorial quality is above average for AI-assisted work.
